To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the vulnerability of large Eurasian perch is determined primarily by spatial habitat choice behaviour, and that the ability of anglers to capture perch is determined by skill but not by the spatial behavioural phenotype of the fish.
the spatial behaviour of perch, and not swimming activity, determines vulnerability to angling, and that angler skill affects catch rates independent of the ability of anglers to encounter fish.

(1) the vulnerability of large perch to angling is strongly determined by a repeatable habitat preference and unrelated to swimming activity, and (2) catch per unit effort increases with self-reported angler skill, an effect not explained by lure choice, but unrelated to the spatial behavioural phenotype of captured fish.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the behaviour of fish and anglers and how they interact in the context of recreational fishing.
the spatial ecology and population genetics of the Eurasian perch (Perca fluviatlis) and the European whitefish (Coregonus lavaretus) and their interactions in the Lake Constance region.
the spatial and behavioural determinants of angler catchability.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
this paper provides a novel insight into the spatial behaviour of a fish species in a natural lake environment and how this relates to angling success.

we have demonstrated that the spatial behaviour of large perch is an important determinant of angling vulnerability, and that the effect of angler skill on angling success is unrelated to the ability of anglers to encounter perch or to the use of different lures, and instead reflects the ability of skilled anglers to exploit spatial behavioural phenotypes of large perch that are more vulnerable to capture.

The study provides an excellent example for a whole-lake experiment that integrates the use of acoustic telemetry and angler behaviour to investigate the interplay between spatial behaviour and fishing success.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
angler skill is not a major determinant of vulnerability in this system, and vulnerability is strongly associated with spatial habitat choice, a repeatable behaviour.
we found that angling vulnerability of large perch in a whole-lakescape was strongly related to the spatial behaviour of the fish.
the fish that are more vulnerable to being captured are the fish that are less active and more likely to stay in the same place.
The main takeaway from our work is that
vulnerability is not simply a function of the fish, nor is it simply a function of angler skill.
the spatial behaviour of fish, rather than the activity level, is a key determinant of vulnerability, and that angler skill is not a proxy of the spatial distribution of vulnerable fish.
vulnerability to capture is not a fixed trait but a function of the interaction between the fish's spatial behaviour and the angler's skill.
